claim: Conservation efforts must be evidence-based, so rapid and economically feasible methods should be used to quantify diversity and distribution patterns.
source: Conservation efforts must be evidence-based, so rapid and economically feasible methods should be used to quantify diversity and distribution patterns.
evidence: This is a statement of principle about conservation methodology presented in the abstract.

claim: The species-rich dataset included ~6500 terminals.
source: The species-rich dataset included ~6500 terminals, ~ 1850 putative species delimited at 5% uncorrected pairwise threshold, possibly ~1000 of them unknown to science.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of terminals in the dataset.

claim: The dataset included ~ 1850 putative species delimited at 5% uncorrected pairwise threshold.
source: The species-rich dataset included ~6500 terminals, ~ 1850 putative species delimited at 5% uncorrected pairwise threshold, possibly ~1000 of them unknown to science.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of putative species identified using a specific threshold.

claim: Possibly ~1000 species in the dataset are unknown to science.
source: The species-rich dataset included ~6500 terminals, ~ 1850 putative species delimited at 5% uncorrected pairwise threshold, possibly ~1000 of them unknown to science.
evidence: Estimation based on comparison of delimited species with known described species.

claim: Neither phylogenomic nor mtDNA data alone could answer questions on biodiversity and phylogeny.
source: Neither type of data could alone answer our questions on biodiversity and phylogeny.
evidence: Statement about the necessity of combining data types for comprehensive analysis.

claim: The phylogenomic backbone enabled the integrative delimitation of robustly defined natural genus-group units.
source: The phylogenomic backbone enabled the integrative delimitation of robustly defined natural genus-group units that will inform future research.
evidence: Statement about the outcome of phylogenomic analysis.

claim: Using constrained mtDNA analysis, the authors identified the spatial structure of species diversity.
source: Using constrained mtDNA analysis, we identified the spatial structure of species diversity, very high species-level endemism, and a biodiversity hotspot in New Guinea.
evidence: Statement about findings from constrained mtDNA analysis.

claim: Very high species-level endemism was identified using constrained mtDNA analysis.
source: Using constrained mtDNA analysis, we identified the spatial structure of species diversity, very high species-level endemism, and a biodiversity hotspot in New Guinea.
evidence: Statement about findings from constrained mtDNA analysis.

claim: New Guinea is a biodiversity hotspot for Metriorrhynchini.
source: Using constrained mtDNA analysis, we identified the spatial structure of species diversity, very high species-level endemism, and a biodiversity hotspot in New Guinea.
evidence: Statement about findings from constrained mtDNA analysis.

claim: The number of known insects surpasses that of all other terrestrial groups.
source: The number of known insects surpasses that of all other terrestrial groups (Mora et al., 2011), and we need much more detailed information to fully understand their diversity.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Mora et al., 2011.

claim: The majority of insect species remain undescribed.
source: Currently, the available biodiversity data are far from complete, and the majority of insect species remain undescribed (Novotny et al., 2006; Srivathsan et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Novotny et al., 2006 and Srivathsan et al., 2019.

claim: Robust phylogenetic hypotheses are lacking for most insect lineages.
source: In addition, robust phylogenetic hypotheses are lacking for most lineages, and the genera and tribes are often artificial assemblages which are not relevant to evolutionary and biodiversity research.
evidence: Statement about the current state of phylogenetic knowledge.

claim: Descriptive, morphology-based insect systematics is not keeping pace with the rapid loss and degradation of natural habitats.
source: Descriptive, morphology-based insect systematics is not keeping pace with the rapid loss and degradation of natural habitats (Theng et al., 2020), and with the ongoing decline in insect abundance as a result of human activities and climate change (van Klink et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Theng et al., 2020 and van Klink et al., 2020.

claim: Zootaxa published almost 30,000 studies describing >60,000 new species in 2001–2020.
source: The largest taxonomic journal, Zootaxa, published almost 30,000 studies describing >60,000 new species and these represent over a quarter of all new animal species reported in 2001–2020 (Zhang, 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Zhang, 2021.

claim: Zootaxa publications represent over a quarter of all new animal species reported in 2001–2020.
source: The largest taxonomic journal, Zootaxa, published almost 30,000 studies describing >60,000 new species and these represent over a quarter of all new animal species reported in 2001–2020 (Zhang, 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Zhang, 2021.

claim: On average, only two new species are reported in a taxonomic publication.
source: Although these numbers are impressive, they also show how labor-intensive is taxonomic research if, in average, only two new species are reported in a publication.
evidence: Calculation based on the numbers provided about Zootaxa publications.

claim: DNA data are indisputably a valuable source for modern biodiversity research.
source: DNA data are indisputably a valuable source for modern biodiversity research, and they can address both shallow and deep relationships (Tautz et al., 2003; Hajibabaei et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Tautz et al., 2003 and Hajibabaei et al., 2007.

claim: DNA data can address both shallow and deep relationships.
source: DNA data are indisputably a valuable source for modern biodiversity research, and they can address both shallow and deep relationships (Tautz et al., 2003; Hajibabaei et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Tautz et al., 2003 and Hajibabaei et al., 2007.

claim: Short fragments are often unsuitable for the building of deep phylogenies.
source: But the short fragments are often unsuitable for the building of deep phylogenies and large genomic datasets need to be used (McKenna et al., 2019; Baca et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to McKenna et al., 2019 and Baca et al., 2021.

claim: Large genomic datasets need to be used for building deep phylogenies.
source: But the short fragments are often unsuitable for the building of deep phylogenies and large genomic datasets need to be used (McKenna et al., 2019; Baca et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to McKenna et al., 2019 and Baca et al., 2021.

claim: Metriorrhynchini contains >1500 recognised species.
source: This net-winged beetle tribe contains >1500 recognised species, mostly found in the Old-World tropics (Figure 1A), and their classification is complicated by the complex taxonomic history (Bocak et al., 2020; see Appendix introductory information).
evidence: Statement about the number of recognized species in the tribe.

claim: Metriorrhynchini are mostly found in the Old-World tropics.
source: This net-winged beetle tribe contains >1500 recognised species, mostly found in the Old-World tropics (Figure 1A), and their classification is complicated by the complex taxonomic history (Bocak et al., 2020; see Appendix introductory information).
evidence: Statement about distribution supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The classification of Metriorrhynchini is complicated by complex taxonomic history.
source: This net-winged beetle tribe contains >1500 recognised species, mostly found in the Old-World tropics (Figure 1A), and their classification is complicated by the complex taxonomic history (Bocak et al., 2020; see Appendix introductory information).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Bocak et al., 2020.

claim: The phenetic plasticity of Metriorrhynchini is relatively high.
source: The phenetic plasticity of Metriorrhynchini is relatively high (Figure 1B–D), but many distant species resemble each other due to convergent selection in Mullerian rings (Bocek et al., 2019; Motyka et al., 2020; Motyka et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by reference to Figure 1B-D.

claim: Many distant Metriorrhynchini species resemble each other due to convergent selection in Mullerian rings.
source: The phenetic plasticity of Metriorrhynchini is relatively high (Figure 1B–D), but many distant species resemble each other due to convergent selection in Mullerian rings (Bocek et al., 2019; Motyka et al., 2020; Motyka et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Bocek et al., 2019; Motyka et al., 2020; Motyka et al., 2021.

claim: There are over 40 genera in the Metriorrhynchini tribe.
source: Although there are over 40 genera in the tribe, three-quarters of the species have been described in five ambiguously defined genera (Xylobanus, Cautires, Trichalus, Metriorrhynchus, and Cladophorus).
evidence: Statement about the number of genera in the tribe.

claim: Three-quarters of Metriorrhynchini species have been described in five ambiguously defined genera.
source: Although there are over 40 genera in the tribe, three-quarters of the species have been described in five ambiguously defined genera (Xylobanus, Cautires, Trichalus, Metriorrhynchus, and Cladophorus).
evidence: Statement about the distribution of species across genera.

claim: Sometimes a single Metriorrhynchini genus contains species from different subtribes.
source: Sometimes a single genus contains species from different subtribes (Bocak et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Bocak et al., 2020.

claim: The authors monitored almost 800 localities.
source: In total, we monitored almost 800 localities, 696 of them with occurrences of the Metriorrhynchini (Tabs. 1, Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Direct statement about the number of localities monitored.

claim: 696 localities had occurrences of Metriorrhynchini.
source: In total, we monitored almost 800 localities, 696 of them with occurrences of the Metriorrhynchini (Tabs. 1, Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Direct statement about the number of localities with Metriorrhynchini.

claim: The densest sampling is available from Sundaland and New Guinea.
source: The densest sampling is available from the Sundaland and New Guinea, while India and the Afrotropical region are under-sampled (Figure 1A).
evidence: Statement about sampling density supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: India and the Afrotropical region are under-sampled.
source: The densest sampling is available from the Sundaland and New Guinea, while India and the Afrotropical region are under-sampled (Figure 1A).
evidence: Statement about sampling density supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The phylogenomic dataset contained 35 Metriorrhynchini terminals.
source: The phylogenomic dataset contained 35 Metriorrhynchini terminals (Appendix 1—table 2), seven outgroups, and ~4200 orthologs (1.9–5.7 × 106 aligned positions; Supplementary file 1; Appendix 1—table 3; Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: Direct statement about the composition of the phylogenomic dataset.

claim: The phylogenomic dataset contained seven outgroups.
source: The phylogenomic dataset contained 35 Metriorrhynchini terminals (Appendix 1—table 2), seven outgroups, and ~4200 orthologs (1.9–5.7 × 106 aligned positions; Supplementary file 1; Appendix 1—table 3; Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: Direct statement about the composition of the phylogenomic dataset.

claim: The phylogenomic dataset contained ~4200 orthologs.
source: The phylogenomic dataset contained 35 Metriorrhynchini terminals (Appendix 1—table 2), seven outgroups, and ~4200 orthologs (1.9–5.7 × 106 aligned positions; Supplementary file 1; Appendix 1—table 3; Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: Direct statement about the composition of the phylogenomic dataset.

claim: Phylogenomic analyses resolved three subtribes: Metanoeina, Metriorrhynchina, and Cautirina.
source: Phylogenomic analyses resolved three subtribes (Metanoeina [Metriorrhynchina, Cautirina]), and five clades were regularly recovered within the Metriorrhynchina, that is, the hereby defined procautirines, leptotrichalines, trichalines, porrostomines, and cladophorines.
evidence: Statement about the results of phylogenomic analyses.

claim: Five clades were regularly recovered within Metriorrhynchina: procautirines, leptotrichalines, trichalines, porrostomines, and cladophorines.
source: Phylogenomic analyses resolved three subtribes (Metanoeina [Metriorrhynchina, Cautirina]), and five clades were regularly recovered within the Metriorrhynchina, that is, the hereby defined procautirines, leptotrichalines, trichalines, porrostomines, and cladophorines.
evidence: Statement about the results of phylogenomic analyses.

claim: All phylogenomic analyses question the definitions of some species rich genera.
source: All phylogenomic analyses question the definitions of some species rich genera (Appendix 1—figures 1–8) that are either polyphyletic (e.g. Cladophorus; 131 described species, most of them recovered in the Ditua subclade) or paraphyletic (Metriorrhynchus as a grade and Porrostoma in the terminal position; 194 species, see Figure 2A and B, Appendix 1—figures 1–8).
evidence: Statement about the results of phylogenomic analyses.

claim: Cladophorus is polyphyletic.
source: All phylogenomic analyses question the definitions of some species rich genera (Appendix 1—figures 1–8) that are either polyphyletic (e.g. Cladophorus; 131 described species, most of them recovered in the Ditua subclade) or paraphyletic (Metriorrhynchus as a grade and Porrostoma in the terminal position; 194 species, see Figure 2A and B, Appendix 1—figures 1–8).
evidence: Statement about the results of phylogenomic analyses.

claim: Cladophorus has 131 described species.
source: All phylogenomic analyses question the definitions of some species rich genera (Appendix 1—figures 1–8) that are either polyphyletic (e.g. Cladophorus; 131 described species, most of them recovered in the Ditua subclade) or paraphyletic (Metriorrhynchus as a grade and Porrostoma in the terminal position; 194 species, see Figure 2A and B, Appendix 1—figures 1–8).
evidence: Statement about the number of described species in Cladophorus.

claim: Most Cladophorus species were recovered in the Ditua subclade.
source: All phylogenomic analyses question the definitions of some species rich genera (Appendix 1—figures 1–8) that are either polyphyletic (e.g. Cladophorus; 131 described species, most of them recovered in the Ditua subclade) or paraphyletic (Metriorrhynchus as a grade and Porrostoma in the terminal position; 194 species, see Figure 2A and B, Appendix 1—figures 1–8).
evidence: Statement about the results of phylogenomic analyses.

claim: Metriorrhynchus is paraphyletic.
source: All phylogenomic analyses question the definitions of some species rich genera (Appendix 1—figures 1–8) that are either polyphyletic (e.g. Cladophorus; 131 described species, most of them recovered in the Ditua subclade) or paraphyletic (Metriorrhynchus as a grade and Porrostoma in the terminal position; 194 species, see Figure 2A and B, Appendix 1—figures 1–8).
evidence: Statement about the results of phylogenomic analyses.

claim: The mtDNA database contained >11,500 mtDNA fragments.
source: The mtDNA database contained >11,500 mtDNA fragments (5935 cox1, 2381 rrnL, and 3205 nad5) representing 6429 terminals (2930 aligned positions).
evidence: Direct statement about the composition of the mtDNA database.

claim: The mtDNA database represented 6429 terminals.
source: The mtDNA database contained >11,500 mtDNA fragments (5935 cox1, 2381 rrnL, and 3205 nad5) representing 6429 terminals (2930 aligned positions).
evidence: Direct statement about the composition of the mtDNA database.

claim: Using 2% and 5% thresholds, 34–37 mOTUs were identified in the Metanoeina clade.
source: Depending on the applied 2% and 5% thresholds, we identified 34–37 mOTUs in the Metanoeina clade and 369–456 mOTUs in Cautirina.
evidence: Statement about the results of mOTU delimitation.

claim: Using 2% and 5% thresholds, 369–456 mOTUs were identified in Cautirina.
source: Depending on the applied 2% and 5% thresholds, we identified 34–37 mOTUs in the Metanoeina clade and 369–456 mOTUs in Cautirina.
evidence: Statement about the results of mOTU delimitation.

claim: The major Metriorrhynchina clade included 1376–1763 mOTUs.
source: The major Metriorrhynchina clade (1376–1763 mOTUs) included procautirines, leptotrichalines, trichalines, porrostomines, and cladophorines.
evidence: Statement about the results of mOTU delimitation.

claim: The kassemiines and five small clades comprised 69–89 mOTUs in total.
source: In addition, we identified several deeply rooted lineages, the kassemiines, and another five small clades (69–89 mOTUs in total; Source data 2), each of which comprised a limited number of species.
evidence: Statement about the results of mOTU delimitation.

claim: The number of mOTUs does not include ~50 mOTUs for which cox1 was unavailable.
source: The number of mOTUs does not include ~50 mOTUs for which cox1 was unavailable.
evidence: Statement about limitations of the mOTU count.

claim: Repeated runs with different starting seeds identified terminals with unstable positions.
source: Repeated runs with different starting seeds identified terminals with unstable positions (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Statement about the results of phylogenetic analyses with reference to Figure 3A-C.

claim: The major clades were generally stable in repeated runs.
source: The major clades were generally stable, whereas small, deeply rooted clades were prone to 'wandering' around the tree, as were distinct singletons.
evidence: Statement about the stability of phylogenetic results.

claim: Small, deeply rooted clades were prone to 'wandering' around the tree.
source: The major clades were generally stable, whereas small, deeply rooted clades were prone to 'wandering' around the tree, as were distinct singletons.
evidence: Statement about the stability of phylogenetic results.

claim: The unconstrained analysis of mitochondrial data yielded a topology with a high number of terminals that were recovered in positions incongruent with their morphology.
source: The unconstrained analysis of mitochondrial data yielded a topology with a high number of terminals that were recovered in positions incongruent with their morphology (Figure 3D and E, Source data 3).
evidence: Statement about the results of unconstrained analysis with reference to Figure 3D and E.

claim: The constrained analysis produced a topology with a much lower proportion of terminals in dubious positions.
source: The same dataset, when analyzed using the constrained position of 35 terminals (based on their relative relationships inferred by prior phylogenomic analyses), produced a topology with a much lower proportion of terminals in dubious positions (Figure 3C, Source data 2).
evidence: Statement about the results of constrained analysis with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: For the Metriorrhynchini, 1848 and 2345 mOTUs were identified using the 5% and 2% thresholds, respectively.
source: For the Metriorrhynchini, we identified 1848 and 2345 mOTUs using the 5% and 2% thresholds, respectively (Appendix 1—figure 14).
evidence: Statement about the results of mOTU delimitation.

claim: Using both 2% and 5% thresholds, the numbers of putative species surpass the numbers of species reported in the literature.
source: Using both thresholds, 2% and 5%, the numbers of putative species surpass the numbers of species reported in the literature.
evidence: Statement comparing mOTU counts to described species.

claim: Only four mOTUs have been recorded in two landmasses separated by a deep-sea (> 200 m).
source: We observed very high species turnover even if 5% threshold was applied for delimitation. Only four mOTUs have been recorded in two landmasses separated by a deep-sea (> 200 m).
evidence: Statement about species turnover and distribution.

claim: Only sixteen mOTUs were distributed across two landmasses separated by an inundated shelf (sea depth <100 m).
source: Similarly, only sixteen mOTUs were distributed across two landmasses separated by an inundated shelf (sea depth <100 m).
evidence: Statement about species turnover and distribution.

claim: New Guinea is a centre of species diversity of the Metriorrhynchini with 1,105 putative species at 5% threshold.
source: The centres of species diversity of the Metriorrhynchini are New Guinea (1,105 putative spp. at 5% threshold) and the seasonally to perennially humid areas of the Sundaland (202 spp. at 5% threshold).
evidence: Statement about species diversity centers.

claim: Sundaland is a centre of species diversity of the Metriorrhynchini with 202 species at 5% threshold.
source: The centres of species diversity of the Metriorrhynchini are New Guinea (1,105 putative spp. at 5% threshold) and the seasonally to perennially humid areas of the Sundaland (202 spp. at 5% threshold).
evidence: Statement about species diversity centers.

claim: The dated subtree indicates the recent origin of morphological divergence in Cautires apterus.
source: The dated subtree indicates the recent origin of morphological divergence (Figure 4A).
evidence: Statement about dating results with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The origin of polymorphism in an unidentified procautirine genus is putatively very recent.
source: The origin of the polymorphism is putatively very recent (Figure 4F).
evidence: Statement about dating results with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: Molecular data cannot replace morphology-based taxonomy.
source: Molecular data cannot replace morphology-based taxonomy (Figure 3C–D; Thomson et al., 2018), but the analyses of our dataset complement and facilitate traditional biodiversity research in several directions.
evidence: Statement about the relationship between molecular and morphological data, supported by citation to Thomson et al., 2018.

claim: The densely sampled phylogeny identifies tribal and generic limits.
source: The densely sampled phylogeny identifies tribal and generic limits.
evidence: Statement about the utility of the phylogeny.

claim: The phylogeny provides a useful foundation for detailed taxonomic research through the identification of weak areas in earlier classifications.
source: It provides a useful foundation for detailed taxonomic research through the identification of weak areas in earlier classifications and points out the clades with undescribed diversity and non-monophyletic genera (e.g. several hundred species of Ditua and paraphyletic Metriorrhynchus; Figure 3, Appendix 1—figure 15).
evidence: Statement about the utility of the phylogeny.

claim: The analyses of species-rich datasets identify the areas with high species diversity as one of the critical conservation value parameters.
source: Furthermore, the analyses of species-rich datasets identify the areas with high species diversity as one of the critical conservation value parameters (Table 2; Baselga, 2010; Srivathsan et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about the utility of the analyses, supported by citations to Baselga, 2010 and Srivathsan et al., 2019.

claim: Traditional taxonomic research costs time and money.
source: Traditional taxonomic research costs time and money, and the number of newly described species is relatively low if we consider the enormous diversity of tropical insects (Novotny et al., 2006; Sangster and Luksenburg, 2015).
evidence: Statement about the limitations of traditional taxonomy, supported by citations to Novotny et al., 2006 and Sangster and Luksenburg, 2015.

claim: The number of newly described species is relatively low considering the enormous diversity of tropical insects.
source: Traditional taxonomic research costs time and money, and the number of newly described species is relatively low if we consider the enormous diversity of tropical insects (Novotny et al., 2006; Sangster and Luksenburg, 2015).
evidence: Statement about the limitations of traditional taxonomy, supported by citations to Novotny et al., 2006 and Sangster and Luksenburg, 2015.

claim: A high turnover indicates a large proportion of hidden diversity, especially in tropical mountains.
source: A high turnover indicates a large proportion of hidden diversity, especially in tropical mountains (Merckx et al., 2015; Mastretta-Yanes et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Merckx et al., 2015 and Mastretta-Yanes et al., 2018.

claim: Mountain fauna is especially vulnerable to climate change.
source: Mountain fauna is especially vulnerable to climate change and its inventorying is urgently needed.
evidence: Statement about the vulnerability of mountain fauna.

claim: 302 Metriorrhynchini species have been described over the past three decades.
source: The Metriorrhynchini has recently received considerable attention in taxonomic studies, and 302 species have been described by several authors over the past three decades, making a total of 1574 formally described species (Table 1, Kazantsev, 2010; Bocak et al., 2020; Appendix introductory information).
evidence: Statement about recent taxonomic activity.

claim: There are 1574 formally described Metriorrhynchini species in total.
source: The Metriorrhynchini has recently received considerable attention in taxonomic studies, and 302 species have been described by several authors over the past three decades, making a total of 1574 formally described species (Table 1, Kazantsev, 2010; Bocak et al., 2020; Appendix introductory information).
evidence: Statement about the total number of described species.

claim: The distance-based analysis indicates the presence of almost 2000 mOTUs.
source: Although the recent 24% increase in described diversity appears substantial, the distance-based analysis indicates the presence of almost 2000 mOTUs (Appendix 1—figure 14).
evidence: Statement about the results of distance-based analysis.

claim: An additional ~50 putative species (494 terminals) were identified based on divergent morphology because of the absence of cox1.
source: An additional ~50 putative species (494 terminals) were identified, but this identification was only based on divergent morphology because of the absence of cox1.
evidence: Statement about additional species identified.

claim: The sampling represents less than 50% of all known species.
source: We assume that our sampling represents only a subset of all known species (< 50%).
evidence: Estimation based on comparison of sampled and described species.

claim: The dataset contains ~1000 undescribed species.
source: It means that the dataset contains ~1000 undescribed species.
evidence: Estimation based on comparison of mOTUs and described species.

claim: At the current rate, formal morphological descriptions of an additional 1000 species would take decades or hundreds of years.
source: At the current rate, formal morphological descriptions of an additional 1000 species would take decades or hundreds of years.
evidence: Projection based on current rates of species description.

claim: Currently undocumented diversity might be lost long before it can be catalogued.
source: This is a very long time in the context of the ongoing deforestation and fragmentation of natural habitats, and currently undocumented diversity might be lost long before it can be catalogued (Brooks et al., 2002; Sodhi et al., 2004; Ceballos et al., 2015; Theng et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2002; Sodhi et al., 2004; Ceballos et al., 2015; Theng et al., 2020.

claim: The rapid DNA-based inventory is an effective shortcut for obtaining basic information on the true diversity of tropical beetles.
source: The rapid DNA-based inventory is an effective shortcut for obtaining basic information on the true diversity of tropical beetles and for setting a benchmark for future biodiversity re-evaluations.
evidence: Statement about the utility of DNA-based inventory.

claim: Tropical rainforests currently cover most of New Guinea.
source: Tropical rainforests currently cover most of New Guinea, a tectonically young island that has not been considered a biodiversity hotspot for vertebrates (Myers et al., 2000; Hall, 2011; Toussaint et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about the current state of New Guinea.

claim: New Guinea has not been considered a biodiversity hotspot for vertebrates.
source: Tropical rainforests currently cover most of New Guinea, a tectonically young island that has not been considered a biodiversity hotspot for vertebrates (Myers et al., 2000; Hall, 2011; Toussaint et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Myers et al., 2000; Hall, 2011; Toussaint et al., 2014.

claim: The New Guinean net-winged beetle fauna is phylogenetically diverse, spatially heterogeneous, and extremely rich.
source: In the case of net-winged beetles, we show that the New Guinean fauna is phylogenetically diverse, spatially heterogeneous, and extremely rich as regards both the number of species and the endemic genera (Table 1).
evidence: Statement about the characteristics of the New Guinean fauna.

claim: The large clades of New Guinean species indicate that the diversification of major lineages preceded the uplift of the islands.
source: Additionally, the large clades of New Guinean species indicate that the diversification of major lineages preceded the uplift of the islands, and possibly started on the northern margin of the Australian craton and adjacent islands.
evidence: Inference based on phylogenetic patterns.

claim: Southeast Asia is a centre of phylogenetic diversity at the tribal level.
source: Southeast Asia is a centre of phylogenetic diversity at the tribal level; its fauna contains all principal lineages and the highest diversity of Cautirina but is smaller than those of New Guinea.
evidence: Statement about the characteristics of the Southeast Asian fauna.

claim: The Afrotropical and Palearctic regions represent only recently populated low-diversity outposts.
source: The Afrotropical and Palearctic regions represent only recently populated low-diversity outposts.
evidence: Statement about the characteristics of the Afrotropical and Palearctic faunas.

claim: Detailed data on Metriorrhynchini diversity indicate low dispersal propensity.
source: Detailed data on Metriorrhynchini diversity indicate low dispersal propensity and this makes Metriorrhynchini a promising model for biogeographic studies (Ikeda et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about dispersal propensity supported by citation to Ikeda et al., 2012.

claim: The densely sampled phylogeny did not find any long-distance dispersal events.
source: Our densely sampled phylogeny did not find any long-distance dispersal events, in contrast to many studies of flying beetles (Balke et al., 2009; Jordal, 2015).
evidence: Statement about dispersal patterns supported by citations to Balke et al., 2009 and Jordal, 2015.

claim: Most recovered overseas dispersal events are limited to distances of less than 100 km and are commonly accompanied by speciation.
source: Most recovered overseas dispersal events are limited to distances of less than 100 km and are commonly accompanied by speciation (Source data 2 and 3).
evidence: Statement about dispersal patterns.

claim: The high proportion of erroneous placement of many taxa renders the distribution data cited in previous literature unsuitable for phylogeographic investigations.
source: The high proportion of erroneous placement of many taxa (Appendix 1—figure 15; Bocak et al., 2020) renders the distribution data cited in previous literature unsuitable for phylogeographic investigations, and revision of the classification is important in order to understand the true distribution of individual taxa.
evidence: Statement about the limitations of previous literature data.

claim: Net-winged beetles include several lineages in which females have lost the ability to completely metamorphose.
source: Net-winged beetles include several lineages in which females have lost the ability to completely metamorphose (Bocak et al., 2008; Mcmahon and Hayward, 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Bocak et al., 2008 and Mcmahon and Hayward, 2016.

claim: Cautires apterus may be the youngest neotenic taxon of all net-winged beetles (36.1 my).
source: We used our data to place the East African Cautires apterus in a phylogenetic context, and the results indicated that it may be the youngest neotenic taxon of all net-winged beetles (36.1 my, Figure 4).
evidence: Statement about dating results with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The extensive DNA database identified an extreme and previously unknown aposematic dimorphism in New Guinean metriorrhynchines.
source: Our extensive DNA database of metriorrhynchine diversity may also play an important role in the study of the evolution of mimicry. Our inventory identified an extreme and previously unknown aposematic dimorphism in New Guinean metriorrhynchines (Figure 4; Figure 5).
evidence: Statement about the discovery of dimorphism with reference to Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The shift to dimorphism was very recent (3.0 mya at the earliest).
source: The placement of sexually dimorphic species in the phylogeny suggests that the shift to dimorphism was very recent (3.0 mya at the earliest) and began when both sexes were small-bodied.
evidence: Statement about dating results.

claim: Mimetic sexual polymorphism is well understood in butterflies with non-mimetic males and mimetic females.
source: Mimetic sexual polymorphism is well understood in butterflies with non-mimetic males and mimetic females (Kunte, 2008), but the advergence of males and females to different aposematic models has only recently been reported in two subfamilies of net-winged beetles (Motyka et al., 2018; Motyka et al., 2020; Motyka et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Kunte, 2008; Motyka et al., 2018; Motyka et al., 2020; Motyka et al., 2021.

claim: The advergence of males and females to different aposematic models has only recently been reported in two subfamilies of net-winged beetles.
source: Mimetic sexual polymorphism is well understood in butterflies with non-mimetic males and mimetic females (Kunte, 2008), but the advergence of males and females to different aposematic models has only recently been reported in two subfamilies of net-winged beetles (Motyka et al., 2018; Motyka et al., 2020; Motyka et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Motyka et al., 2018; Motyka et al., 2020; Motyka et al., 2021.

claim: Divergent evolution in Müllerian systems appears to be more common in multi-pattern aposematic rings than was previously believed.
source: Divergent evolution in Müllerian systems appears to be more common in multi-pattern aposematic rings than was previously believed when morphology was the sole source of information.
evidence: Inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: Priority areas for global conservation have usually been identified based on richness, species endemism and vulnerability of vertebrates.
source: Priority areas for global conservation have usually been identified based on richness, species endemism and vulnerability of vertebrates (Myers et al., 2000; Holt et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Myers et al., 2000 and Holt et al., 2013.

claim: Different patterns of biodiversity distribution can be revealed if other animal groups are studied.
source: We assume that different patterns of biodiversity distribution can be revealed if other animal groups are studied.
evidence: Assumption based on the findings of the study.

claim: Beetles are the most speciose group of animals but are much less known than vertebrates.
source: Our model, beetles, is the most speciose group of animals but is much less known than vertebrates.
evidence: Statement about the relative knowledge of beetles compared to vertebrates.

claim: The constrained position of less than 2% terminals increases the stability of tree topology.
source: We show that the constrained position of less than 2% terminals increases the stability of tree topology and the congruence of molecular hypotheses with morphological traits (Appendix results).
evidence: Statement about the results of constrained analysis.

claim: The constrained position of less than 2% terminals increases the congruence of molecular hypotheses with morphological traits.
source: We show that the constrained position of less than 2% terminals increases the stability of tree topology and the congruence of molecular hypotheses with morphological traits (Appendix results).
evidence: Statement about the results of constrained analysis.

claim: The voucher-based DNA entries established a framework for classifying samples from other studies, such as environmental sequencing.
source: The voucher-based DNA entries established a framework for classifying samples from other studies, such as environmental sequencing (Linard et al., 2016; Andújar et al., 2015; Arribas et al., 2016) and for subsequent morphology-based studies.
evidence: Statement about the utility of voucher-based DNA entries, supported by citations to Linard et al., 2016; Andújar et al., 2015; Arribas et al., 2016.

claim: The literature records of tropical beetles cannot be used for biodiversity conservation and metanalyses without critical revision.
source: Our large-scale inventory shows that the literature records of tropical beetles cannot be used for biodiversity conservation and metanalyses without critical revision.
evidence: Statement about the limitations of literature records.

claim: Focused field research and subsequent workflow steps can set a benchmark for future evaluation of spatiotemporal changes in biodiversity.
source: We suggest that if focused field research is conducted even by a small research group and subsequent workflow steps are applied to any hyperdiverse tropical group, the results can set a benchmark for future evaluation of spatiotemporal changes in biodiversity.
evidence: Suggestion based on the findings of the study.

claim: About 10% of samples were provided by other researchers.
source: About 10% of samples were provided by other researchers.
evidence: Statement about the source of samples.

claim: Tissues for transcriptomic analyses were fixed in the field.
source: Tissues for transcriptomic analyses were fixed in the field.
evidence: Statement about the methods used.

claim: About 100 tissue samples were fixed and thirty-five of them were used for sequencing.
source: About 100 tissue samples were fixed and thirty-five of them were used for sequencing (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: Statement about the number of samples used for sequencing.

claim: Almost 7000 samples from 696 localities were included in the sequencing program to obtain short mtDNA fragments.
source: Almost 7000 samples from 696 localities (Table 1) were included in the sequencing program to obtain short mtDNA fragments.
evidence: Statement about the number of samples sequenced.

claim: 6429 samples yielding at least a single fragment were included in the analysis.
source: In total, 6429 yielding at least a single fragment were included in the analysis (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Statement about the number of samples included in the analysis.

claim: Libraries for thirty transcriptomes were prepared by Novogene Co., Ltd. and sequenced on the HiSeq X-ten platform.
source: Libraries for thirty transcriptomes were prepared by Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China) and sequenced on the HiSeq X-ten platform (Illumina Inc, San Diego, CA).
evidence: Statement about the methods used for sequencing.

claim: The total DNA of Metanoeus sp. and an unidentified Metriorrhynchina species was shotgun-sequenced on the HiSeq X-ten platform.
source: Additionally, the total DNA (~33 Gb each) of Metanoeus sp. (Voucher code G19002) and an unidentified sample Metriorrhynchina species (Voucher JB0085) was shotgun-sequenced on the same platform.
evidence: Statement about the methods used for sequencing.

claim: The ortholog set was collated by searching the OrthoDB 9.1 for single copy orthologs in six beetle genomes.
source: The ortholog set was collated by searching the OrthoDB 9.1 (Zdobnov et al., 2017) for single copy orthologs in six beetle genomes (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: Statement about the methods used for ortholog identification, supported by citation to Zdobnov et al., 2017.

claim: From the recovered 4193 orthologs, terminal stop codons were removed, and internal stop codons at the translational and nucleotide levels were masked.
source: From the recovered 4193 orthologs, terminal stop codons were removed, and internal stop codons at the translational and nucleotide levels were masked.
evidence: Statement about the data processing methods.

claim: The amino acid sequences were aligned using MAFFT v.7.471 with the L-INS-i algorithm.
source: The amino acid sequences were aligned using MAFFT v.7.471 with the L-INS-i algorithm (Katoh and Standley, 2013).
evidence: Statement about the methods used for alignment, supported by citation to Katoh and Standley, 2013.

claim: The remaining 4109 alignments were retained for subsequent multispecies coalescent analyses.
source: Finally, the remaining 4109 alignments were retained for subsequent multispecies coalescent analyses, and different concatenated datasets were generated for both amino acid and nucleotide levels using FasConCat-G v.1.4 (Kück and Longo, 2014; Appendix 1—table 4 and Appendix methods).
evidence: Statement about the data used for analysis, supported by citation to Kück and Longo, 2014.

claim: Phylogenetic reconstruction was performed using the maximum likelihood (ML) criterion with IQ-TREE 2.1.2.
source: For all datasets, phylogenetic reconstruction was performed using the maximum likelihood (ML) criterion with IQ-TREE 2.1.2 (Minh et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement about the methods used for phylogenetic reconstruction, supported by citation to Minh et al., 2020.

claim: The Accurate Species Tree Algorithm (ASTRAL-III v.5.7.3) was used for coalescent species tree estimation.
source: For subsequent coalescent species tree estimation, the Accurate Species Tree Algorithm (ASTRAL-III v.5.7.3; Zhang et al., 2018) was used.
evidence: Statement about the methods used for coalescent analysis, supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Three fragments of mitochondrial genome were sequenced: cox1+ tRNA Leu+ cox2, rrnL+ tRNA Leu+ nad1, and nad5 and adjacent tRNAs.
source: Three fragments of mitochondrial genome were sequenced: cox1+ tRNA Leu+ cox2 (~1100 bp), rrnL+ tRNA Leu+ nad1 (~800 bp), and ~1210 bp of nad5 and adjacent tRNA-Phe, tRNA-Glu, and tRNA-Ser mtDNA (the mtDNA fragments are further mentioned as rrnL, cox1, and nad5).
evidence: Statement about the mtDNA fragments sequenced.

claim: Altogether 6476 individuals were analyzed including some previously published.
source: Altogether 6476 individuals were analyzed including some previously published (Sklenarova et al., 2013; Bocek and Bocak, 2019).
evidence: Statement about the number of individuals analyzed, supported by citations to Sklenarova et al., 2013 and Bocek and Bocak, 2019.

claim: The cox1 gene fragment was used for OTU delimitation using CD-hit-est and different thresholds.
source: The cox1 gene fragment was used to OTUs delimitation (Blaxter et al., 2005) using CD-hit-est (Fu et al., 2012) and different thresholds (from similarity 0.99–0.90 by 0.05 steps).
evidence: Statement about the methods used for OTU delimitation, supported by citations to Blaxter et al., 2005 and Fu et al., 2012.

claim: The results of the TSA/WGS analyses were used to constrain basal topology among major clades of Metriorrhynchini.
source: The results of the TSA/WGS analyses were used to constrain basal topology among major clades of Metriorrhynchini in both analyses of datasets A and B.
evidence: Statement about the methods used for constrained analysis.

claim: Unconstrained analyses of the datasets were run with identical settings except -g option to compare results.
source: Further, we ran unconstrained analyses of the above-mentioned datasets with identical settings except -g option to compare results.
evidence: Statement about the methods used for unconstrained analysis.

claim: Constrained tree search was replicated nineteen-times and resulting trees were compared using Robinson–Foulds distances.
source: We replicated constrained tree search nineteen-times and compared resulting trees using Robinson–Foulds distances in R package phangorn (Schliep, 2011; Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: Statement about the methods used for tree comparison, supported by citation to Schliep, 2011.
